medianFullTime.source: Estimate. The PLFS average for regular wage or salaried workers in calendar 2025 is Rs 21,285 a month (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_in_India; men Rs 24,217, women Rs 18,353 per the MoSPI PLFS Annual Report 2025 press note, https://www.mospi.gov.in/uploads/latestReleases/latest_release_1774607827733_3e8964a9-268b-4cc9-ad65-cfc8a9e32f08_Press_note_AR_PLFS_2025_23032025_V2.1_26032026_final.pdf). Mean is Rs 21,285 x 12 = Rs 255,420 a year. The median is not published in what I could reach; assumed about 0.82 x the mean, roughly Rs 17,500 a month x 12 = Rs 210,000. Casual workers have a median near Rs 9,000 a month (https://www.dataforindia.com/salaried-jobs/).

p90FullTime.source: Estimate, not verified. The 90th percentile of regular wage or salaried pay is assumed to be about 2.3 x the PLFS mean of Rs 21,285 a month, roughly Rs 50,000 a month x 12 = Rs 600,000. No published PLFS percentile figure was reachable. Consistent with mid-level software engineers (about Rs 1.1 million) being above the 90th percentile and mid-career mechanical engineers (about Rs 520,000) being near it.

livingCost.source: Numbeo India (30 Sep 2026): one-bedroom flat outside the city centre Rs 8,721/month, utilities Rs 3,604, monthly transport pass Rs 800, single-person costs excluding rent Rs 27,576 at mid-range spending (https://numbeo.com/cost-of-living/country_result.jsp?country=India). A modest budget of about Rs 22,000/month net (rent Rs 8,700, food and utilities about Rs 10,000, transport and phone about Rs 3,000) is Rs 264,000 a year; grossed up by about 12% for provident fund and minimal tax gives about Rs 300,000.
livingCost.basis: Single adult in a typical (tier-2 or outer-metro) city: shared or modest one-room rent outside the centre, home-cooked food, bus or metro, about Rs 22,000 a month net, grossed up for 12% provident fund.

tuition.notes: All amounts are annual fees for a typical domestic student in rupees, tuition plus compulsory institute fees, excluding hostel and mess. India has no community colleges, so community means open or low-cost institutions (government degree colleges, IGNOU, ITIs). State means mainstream public universities (state and central universities, government colleges). Elite means Institutes of National Importance and top National Law Universities (IIT, IIM, AIIMS, NLU). Medicine is mapped by selectivity, not cost: the hardest-to-enter government colleges (AIIMS, MAMC) are cheapest, and private colleges are the most expensive. IIT fees are waived fully for SC/ST/PwD and cut by two-thirds for family income Rs 1-5 lakh. Loans at elite colleges are common.

nominalRate.source: SBI education loan schemes, rates from 9 June 2026 (https://sbi.bank.in/web/interest-rates/interest-rates/loan-schemes-interest-rates/education-loan-scheme): Student Loan 9.40% with collateral over Rs 7.5 lakh and 9.90% without collateral up to Rs 7.5 lakh; mean rate of interest Q1 FY27 9.31%; PM-Vidyalaxmi schemes 6.90% / 7.20% / 8.40%; premier-institute concession 6.75%. Value is percent per year, floating, linked to an external benchmark of 7.90% (repo 5.25% + 2.65% spread).

inflation.source: MoSPI headline CPI inflation, August 2026 = 4.82% (July 4.45%) (https://indiainflation.com/, https://www.finnovate.in/learn/blog/india-cpi-inflation-august-2026). Value is percent per year.

studentLoan.description: There is no income-contingent scheme. Students borrow from public-sector banks such as SBI at floating rates. The PM-Vidyalaxmi scheme (collateral-free and guarantee-backed for students admitted to about 860-966 selected institutions; SBI rates 6.90-8.40%) is the main public scheme; the standard SBI Student Loan is 9.4-9.9%. Girl students get a 0.50% concession. Real rate is about 9.3 - 4.82 = 4.5% a year at the typical rate. Both rate values here are percent, not fractions.

schooling.primarySchool: Prathamik Vidyalaya (प्राथमिक विद्यालय), primary school, Classes 1-5, ages 6-11 (under NEP 2020 the 'Foundational' stage also covers ages 3-8 with pre-school)
schooling.middleSchool: Uchch Prathamik (upper primary, Classes 6-8, ages 11-14), then Madhyamik Vidyalaya (माध्यमिक विद्यालय, secondary, Classes 9-10, ages 14-16), ending with the Class 10 board exam (CBSE AISSE or state 'Matric'/SSC)
schooling.schoolLeaving: Senior Secondary Certificate, the Class 12 board exam (CBSE AISSCE or state boards, 'Bārahvīṃ'), taken at about 17-18; university entry mostly by separate entrance exams (JEE for IITs, NEET for medicine, CUET for central universities, CLAT for law)
schooling.vocational: ITI (Industrial Training Institute, आईटीआई), 1-2 year trade courses after Class 8 or 10; Polytechnic diploma, 3 years after Class 10 (lateral entry into engineering degrees)
schooling.tierCommunity: Government degree college or open university (IGNOU)
schooling.tierState: State or central university (for example Delhi University, University of Mumbai)
schooling.tierElite: IIT, IIM, AIIMS, NLU (Institutes of National Importance and National Law Universities)
schooling.gradeSystem: Each subject is marked out of 100 and the overall result is quoted as a percentage. Higher is better. The pass mark is 33% in each subject, and 33% separately in theory and practical where both apply. Subjects also get letter grades A1 to E by rank among those who passed: A1 is the top 1/8, D2 the bottom 1/8, E means fail. In 2026 the CBSE Class 12 pass rate was 85.20% (88.39% in 2025); 1,507,109 of 1,768,968 candidates passed. A typical passing result is roughly 70-80% (my estimate, not verified), 90% and above is a top result, and 95-100% is exceptional. Elite programmes (IIT, AIIMS, NLU) also require a high rank in a separate entrance exam, so the board percentage alone does not get a place.
schooling.startingAges: Primary starts at 6 (Class 1) and ends at 11; lower secondary (Classes 6-10) runs 11-16 with the Class 10 board exam at about 15-16; upper secondary (Classes 11-12) runs 16-18. Students choose a stream (Science, Commerce or Arts) at Class 11, so the main track split is at about 16. The 2020 education policy restructures school as 5+3+3+4, starting at age 3. Bachelor's degrees start at about 18 (3-4 years; 4 for engineering, 5.5 for MBBS).

highlights: There is no single national minimum wage: Delhi's unskilled rate is ₹18,456 a month, Uttar Pradesh's is ₹11,314, and a regular salaried worker averages ₹21,285 a month.
IIT tuition is ₹2 lakh a year, but a seat at a government medical college such as Maulana Azad costs only about ₹2,700 a year (₹12,225 for the whole degree).
caveats: WebSearch hit its session cap (200 of 200) after 6 of my searches, so the rest came from direct page fetches with no search-engine discovery. Many salary figures are therefore from Indeed, PayScale and Talent.com, which skew to private-sector, urban, self-reported pay and sometimes rest on very few salaries (Indeed pilot, first officer, sales director, police). Figures marked low are my estimates or blends and should be reviewed. Every rupee figure is annual gross in Rs. Both the student-loan rate and inflation are given in percent (9.3 and 4.82), not as fractions. Specific weak spots. (1) National median and 90th percentile are my estimates derived from the PLFS mean of Rs 21,285 a month (calendar 2025, Wikipedia quoting PLFS; men and women figures confirmed in the MoSPI press note); I found no published median or percentile. Informal and casual workers (about half the workforce) are far below that. (2) Minimum wage: India has no single binding national figure (floor wage is Rs 178 a day and non-binding). I used Delhi (Rs 18,456/month from April 2025; an October 2025 revision circulating online was denounced as forged, and April 2026 was still awaited) as a capital-city level. Other states are much lower: Uttar Pradesh Rs 11,314, Bihar Rs 11,336, Maharashtra Zone I Rs 13,921, West Bengal Rs 10,383 (https://www.india-briefing.com/news/guide-minimum-wage-india-19406.html/), so Rs 221,472 sits above my Rs 200,000 cashier median. If the game floors offers at the minimum, use a state-typical figure (about Rs 13,900 a month = Rs 167,000 a year) to avoid lifting cashier pay above the market. One labourcodecalc.in page lists Delhi at Rs 783 a day (Rs 20,358 a month), which I could not confirm and did not use. (3) Public versus private pay gap: government posts (teachers, nurses, doctors, police on 7th Pay Commission scales with 60% dearness allowance from January 2026) pay several times the private-market figures from the job sites. The 8th Pay Commission is pending. My teacher, nurse, doctor and police numbers are blends. Government scales would suggest secondary teacher Rs 9-12 lakh, specialist doctor about Rs 22-24 lakh. (4) IIT fees: most sources say Rs 2 lakh a year tuition; CollegeDekho lists IIT Delhi at Rs 1 lakh a year. Elite fee remissions by family income exist. (5) Medicine tier mapping: I mapped by selectivity, so community = private colleges (about Rs 12 lakh a year), state = state government colleges (about Rs 60,000), elite = AIIMS/MAMC (about Rs 2,700). This is the reverse of the fee ordering used for bachelors, so check how the game reads tiers. (6) Tuition for vocational, community and state master and doctorate, state medicine and community and state law are unverified estimates. (7) Airline captain rests on 8 PayScale profiles (Jan 2025); first officer is about half of that by my estimate; CEO pay is a large-cap estimate of Rs 10 crore with no sourced figure. (8) FX is 96.095 per USD on 30 Sep 2026 and the rupee lost about 8.4% in 12 months, so USD conversions of local pay have shifted since 2025 while the PPP factor (20.09) did not. (9) Student loan: rates are for SBI; other public banks are similar. The claim about the PM-Vidyalaxmi institution count is from memory, not fetched. No government interest subsidy is reflected in the rate (the scheme's subvention for lower-income families was not verified). (10) Grade-scale 'typical 70-80%' is my estimate.
